concoct

/kun-KOKT/ - the stress falls on KOKT · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Concoct means to make up an untrue account.

Rather than confess he had forgotten the anniversary, he concocted a tale about a marvelous surprise that had 'fallen through at the last minute.'

Example

The stowaway concocted an entire biography between decks — a sick brother in the capital, a job waiting at the ironworks — and held the invention together through six days of questioning.

Concoct is kitchen vocabulary: a story thrown together from whatever ingredients are at hand. To overstate is to heat the truth and to fudge is to blur it — to concoct is to cook a dish that was never on the menu, an account with no true events in it at all.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

cook up: Cook up is the informal twin of concoct — same kitchen, same dishonest recipe, a story thrown together fast when the truth is inconvenient. Concoct is the slightly dressier word a novelist or a narrator reaches for; cook up is what the culprit's friends would say.

dream up: To dream up is to invent something new — a gadget, a game, a plot for a film — with no dishonesty implied at all. Concoct points the invention at deception: a concocted account is assembled from nothing precisely so that someone will mistake it for the truth.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

recount: retell events exactly as they happened

own up: admit the awkward truth instead of inventing around it

Where it sits · how far the story departs from fact — overstate → fudge → concoct

overstate vs. concoct: Overstate is the mildest rung, well below concoct — an overstated report heats up real events, but real events are still in the pan.

fudge vs. concoct: Fudge stops short of concoct: to fudge is to blur or nudge true numbers, while to concoct is to cook the entire dish from nothing.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — con-

Prefix — con-: together

Root — coct-

Root — coct-: cooked (Latin coquere, 'to cook')

Put it together

Put it together: Latin coquere meant 'to cook,' and concoquere was to cook ingredients down together. English kept the kitchen: to concoct is to throw whatever is at hand into the pot — and when the dish is a story, the ingredients are inventions. The root still steams in biscuit, literally 'twice-cooked.'

Use the root in a new word: biscuit

Use the root in a new word: biscuit: Ships' biscuit was baked hard enough to survive a year at sea.

Word Choice

neutral / lightly comic

Concoct is for stories assembled fast out of nothing, and it often carries a smile at the teller's expense. Fabricate, its neighbor in this unit, is colder and more deliberate — data, evidence, whole ledgers. If someone merely stretched real events, overstate is the fairer word.
